title: Case automation under integration batches: CPU limit refactor in 4 stages

stages.scenario: An after-save record-triggered Flow on Case sets priority and routing fields on the triggering Case and creates a follow-up Task. A 200-Case Data Loader update fails with Apex CPU time limit exceeded, and the debug log shows the Case triggers running twice. What is the root cause?

options.text: The Flow updates the triggering Case after save, so the save order runs again
options.coachingFeedback: Changing the record that started the transaction from an after-save context issues a second DML, which re-executes the save order and fires every trigger and flow again. That second pass is why the triggers appear twice and CPU time doubles.

options.text: The Case trigger has no static recursion guard, so it re-enters when the Flow saves
options.coachingFeedback: A guard would stop the trigger body from running twice, but the Flow's second DML still re-runs validation, flows, and other automation in the save order. It treats the symptom, not the extra save.

options.text: The Task creation runs inside the Case transaction instead of on an asynchronous path
options.coachingFeedback: Moving the Task out would trim some work, but inserting related Tasks does not make the Case triggers run twice; the repeated save of the Case itself does.

stages.scenario: The Case automation sets priority and routing fields on the triggering Case and creates a Task for escalated Cases. Integrations send updates of up to 200 Cases several times an hour. Which design should replace the Flow?

options.text: Keep the after-save Flow and add entry conditions so it runs only when routing inputs change
options.coachingFeedback: Entry conditions cut runs on irrelevant edits, but every Case that does match still saves twice, so integration batches of routing changes hit the same CPU cost.

options.text: A before-save Flow for the Case fields and a separate after-save Flow for the Task
options.coachingFeedback: Same-record changes made before save are written in memory and committed with the original DML, so the save order runs once. The Task is a related record, which needs the after-save context, and splitting well-conditioned flows costs little performance.

options.text: Move both the field updates and the Task creation onto the Flow's Run Asynchronously path
options.coachingFeedback: The async path runs after commit in a separate transaction, so updating the Case there still triggers a second save, and routing fields are missing when the integration's call returns. It also shares the daily async flow limits and is not meant for high-volume processing.

stages.scenario: The new flows pass a full-sandbox regression. Integration users update Cases around the clock, and the old and new flows set the same routing fields. How should the team cut over?

options.text: Gate old and new flows on one custom permission, assigned to one integration user first
options.coachingFeedback: Entry conditions that check a custom permission let a permission set assignment choose which automation runs for each user, with no deployment. One integration user proves the new path under production load, and removing the assignment is the rollback.

options.text: Deactivate the old Flow and activate the new ones together during the lowest-volume hour
options.coachingFeedback: A single switch exposes every integration to the new logic at once, and a defect found later means reactivating the old version by hand while updates keep arriving around the clock.

options.text: Activate the new flows alongside the old Flow for a week and compare the values they set
options.coachingFeedback: Both sets of flows write the same routing fields, so each change is applied twice and the old Flow keeps causing the second save the refactor exists to remove.

stages.scenario: After cutover, the team wants warning before a larger integration batch or a new Case automation pushes Case saves toward the CPU limit. What should the team monitor?

options.text: Apex exception emails sent to the admin whenever a Case transaction hits a limit
options.coachingFeedback: Exception emails arrive only after a batch has already rolled back, so they report failures rather than the approach to the limit.

options.text: Daily API request usage for the integration users on the System Overview page
options.coachingFeedback: API usage counts calls, not the work each call triggers; a 200-Case update costs the same requests whether its save uses little CPU or nearly all of it.

options.text: CPU time per Case transaction from Event Monitoring, alerting well before the limit
options.coachingFeedback: Event Monitoring's Apex Execution logs record CPU time per transaction, so the trend shows headroom shrinking before anything fails. Alerting near 70% of the limit keeps a 30% reserve for spikes.
